This vignette will showcase all of the basic functionality found in the `varkit` package.

## Setup

We start off by loading the package and defining the path to the VCF file we
wish to load. The file can be either compressed or uncompressed, but for this
example we will use a block-gzipped VCF:

```{r setup}
library(varkit)

# This might need to be increased for large VCFs
Sys.setenv("VROOM_CONNECTION_SIZE" = 1e6)

path <- system.file("extdata", "celegans.vcf.bgz", package = "varkit")
```

> NOTE: if you want to use `tidyverse` or more specifically `stringr`, it is
> recommended to load that library first. Due to the collision with the
> `fixed()` function.

## Loading a VCF into R

In it's simplest form you would load a VCF file into memory like so:

```{r read_simple, eval = FALSE}
vcf <- read_vcf(path, ploidy = 2)
```

However, it is good practice to first validate if the VCF header is parsed correctly:

```{r header}
header <- read_vcf_header(path)
print(header)
```

> NOTE: Many VarKit functions return a 'tibble', which can be treated as a regular
> `data.frame`, but it displays more compactly when printed to the console.

The most important information here is the column names, which are printed last
(located under `header$col_names`). If the VCF file is recognised correctly it
should list all of the fixed fields and samples present in your VCF. The column
names listed in the header can be provided to the `read_vcf()` function in order
to exclude them. This is useful if you want to exclude specific samples, or if
you know you are not going to use certain fixed fields and want to save memory.

For example here we exclude the "INFO" and "FILTER" fixed fields and the sample "N2":

```{r read}
vcf <- read_vcf(path, ploidy = 2, skip_cols = c("info", "filter", "N2"))
print(vcf)
```

## Accessing specific fields

The `read_vcf()` function returns a special "varkit" object that holds all of
the information parsed from the VCF. This information should be accessed through
designated functions, the most important of which are:

```{r access}
samples(vcf)

fixed(vcf)

geno(vcf)
```

> This syntax is similar to for example accessing the column names of a data
> frame `colnames(df)`.

## Getting help

Functions like `read_vcf()`, `read_vcf_header()`, and `geno()` return objects
with special classes, giving them access to an array of build-in functions. To
check which functions are available for any given object use the `vakit_help()`
function:

```{r help}
varkit_help(vcf)
```

## Accessing header metadata

In this example, the header metadata can be accessed both from the `vcf` and
`header` objects, like so:

```{r metdata}
meta(vcf) # OR meta(header)
```

However, you might notice that although the returned object is a data frame,
most of the information stored in the `$value` column and cannot be easily
accessed. VarKit provides a function to parse these values, but this requires
you to select the type of field that should be parsed. You can get an overview
of the available field types using:

```{r meta_summary}
get_meta_types(vcf)
```

Using this information we can then use the `parse_meta_type()` function to
parse the metadata of a specific type. For example we can lookup what the
different values in the INFO fields mean, or we can access the size of the
contigs:

```{r meta_parse}
parse_meta_type(vcf, "INFO")

parse_meta_type(vcf, "contig")
```

## Masking

A common operation when working with VCF is removing specific sites, based on
various criteria. In VarKit this is achieved through the `mask()` function, which
either requires you to input a logical vector (TRUE if the site should be
masked) or a data frame with columns "chorm" and "pos" containing the sites to
be masked. For this example we will use a logical vector to mask/hide all sites on
chromosome I:

```{r mask}
# This is a logical vector
mask_site <- fixed(vcf)$chrom == "I"

# Be sure to reassign the returned object to `vcf` otherwise the mask will not take effect
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = mask_site)

# Use the summary function to check the number of visible sites
summary(vcf)
```

Now if we fetch data from the VCF object the masked sites will no longer be
returned. For example if we retrieve the fixed fields we can see that the sites
with CHROM = "I" are missing (if you look back, you can see that they were
previously on top):

```{r mask_check}
fixed(vcf)
```

It is important to note that masking can be performed multiple times in
sequence, which will cause sites in **either** mask to be excluded:

```{r mask_seq}
# Let's use a data frame this time around
sites_to_mask <- dplyr::filter(fixed(vcf), qual < 3000)
nrow(sites_to_mask)
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = sites_to_mask)
summary(vcf)
```

You can see that this filter masked an additional 3 sites.

### Masking sites without variation

A common task after subsetting or converting VCF files is removing/masking sites
that no longer contain variation. VarKit provides a convenient function to achieve
this:

```{r mask_variation}
vcf <- mask_sites_without_variation(vcf)
summary(vcf)
```

If you compare with the previous `summary()` you can see that 1 additional site was
masked because it lacked variation.

### Using multiple masks

This process is called 'masking' not 'removing' sites, because the sites are not
actually removed from memory, they are just skipped by the VarKit functions.
This allows you to quickly unmask sites or restore an exported set of masked sites.

In this example we will fist export the mask we just created (which masks sites
on CHROM = "I" or sites with a QUAL < 3000) and assign it to the `my_mask`
variable, then we will remove the mask from the vcf object which verify through
the `summary()` function:

```{r mask_export}
my_mask <- export_mask(vcf)
vcf <- unmask_all(vcf)
summary(vcf)
```

Then if we later decide that we need the mask again, we can import it:

```{r mask_import}
vcf <- import_mask(vcf, my_mask)
summary(vcf)
```

In this way you could use different masks for different parts of your
analysis/script.

### Removing sites

In some cases, e.g. when you need to free memory or when you need maximum
lookup speed, it is possible to entirely remove sites (meaning they cannot be
retrieved by unmasking):

```{r mask_remove}
reduced_vcf <- remove_masked(vcf)
summary(reduced_vcf)
```

## Writing VCF files

Varkit also has the ability to write VCF files. This is useful for example when
you have removed specific sites or samples and want to write the reduced file.

Moreover, masks are also stored in the FILTER column of the resulting VCF file
if `replace_filter = TRUE`, allowing you to save and load a masked VCF:

```{r mask_save}
temp_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".vcf.bz2")
write_vcf(vcf, path = temp_file, replace_filter = TRUE)

read_vcf(temp_file, ploidy = 2)
```

> NOTE: the `readr` library (which is used internally) does not support writing
> in the block-gzipped format that is expected by many other tools. To achieve
> this you can export to plain ".vcf" and convert the file using the "bgzip"
> CLI (and "tabix" for indexing).

## Detecting linkage between sites

Lastly, the VarKit package provides functions to detect linkage between sites.
These functions use the `stats::cor(..., method = "pearson", use =
"pairwise.complete.obs")` internally, thus you can lookup its documentation for
more information.

In order for this to work `geno(vcf)` should contain only **numeric** values (or
NA). Most likely you genotype fields will be in the string format and thus need
to be converted. How to achieve this is highly circumstantial and will require
manual parsing/conversion. For tips take a look at the "Notes for advanced
users" section at the bottom.

As you might have noticed, the example file contains genotype calls (GT, e.g.
"0/1"), which will first convert to numeric dosages using a hidden function:

```{r convert_geno}
# The function below is not exported as it is not very robust, use it with caution!
vcf$geno <- varkit:::.bi_gt2dosage(vcf$geno)
```

Although you could use the `find_linked_sites()` function directly, on larger
VCF files you can speed up the process by first checking for identical columns
(i.e. R^2^ = 1):

```{r identical_sites, results = 'hide'}
llist <- find_identical_sites(vcf, cores = 1)
```

```{r identical_sites_summary}
summary(llist)
```

This will return a "link_list" object that tracks which sites (using their
index) are linked to each other and contains information on which sites to mask
in order to remove linkage (see also `varkit_help(llist)`). Therefore, we can
use this object to mask sites in order to remove the linkage (this will mask all
but the centre most site out of sets of identical/linked sites):

```{r mask_identical}
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = llist)
summary(vcf)
```

Now that identical sites are masked we can check for linkage on the reduced set
of sites. Here we will use an cutoff of R^2^ = 0.7:

```{r linked_sites, results = 'hide'}
llist <- find_linked_sites(vcf, cutoff = 0.7, window = 5e4, cores = 1)
vcf <- mask(vcf, site = llist)
```

```{r linked_sites_summary}
summary(vcf)
```

It is important to know that `find_indentical_sites()` checks entire
chromosomes/scaffolds, whereas `find_linked_sites()` only checks for linkage
within a specified window (here we use the default of 50,000 bp). To check entire
chromosomes in the latter case set the "window" option to 0 or -1.

> Both of these function support multi-threading through the "cores" option and
> only look for identical/linked columns within chromosomes/scaffolds. To check
> for linkage between all chromosomes set `by_chrom = FALSE`. However, this will
> greatly increase computational load.

### Reading/writing link_list objects to file

It might be interesting to store the information about linked sites as it will
tell you the extend of linkage and which sites are a "proxy" of others:

```{r llist_wirte}
temp_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
write_link_list(llist, path = temp_file)
```

Which can then be read back into memory like so:

```{r llist_read}
llist2 <- read_link_list(temp_file)
summary(llist2)
```

## Notes for advanced users
### Modifying the varkit object directly

It is safe to directly modify the varkit object using the `$` operator as long
as `nrow(vcf$fixed) == ncol(vcf$geno) == length(vcf$use_sites)`, the
`vcf$fixed$chrom` & `vcf$fixed$pos` columns are retained, and `vcf$geno` keeps
the 'varkit_geno' class (the latter may be violated when extracting, e.g.
`geno(vcf)[, 1]`, which will remove the class).

The attentive reader might have noticed that we have already made use of this before:

```{r advanced_example, eval = FALSE}
vcf$geno <- varkit:::.bi_gt2dosage(vcf$geno)
```

To retain the "varkit_geno" class use the `varkit_geno()` function, e.g.:

```{r advanced_geno, eval = FALSE}
vcf$geno <- varkit_geno(my_matrix) # this is an example, my_matrix is not defined here
```

Or use one of the the provided apply wrappers:

```{r apply}
# Here `x` contains all genotypes for a single site (length == # samples)
vcf$geno <- apply_sites(vcf$geno, function(x) x + 1)

# Here `x` contains all genotypes for a sample (length == # sites)
vcf$geno <- apply_samples(vcf$geno, function(x) x - 1)
```

Above we do not use `geno(vcf)` as that function only returns the non-masked sites.

> NOTE: the `apply` wrappers will only retain the "varkit_geno" class if the
> function returns a vector of the same length as the input.

### A closer look into the link_list object

Link_list objects are lists that contain a 0 if the site at the matching index
is not linked to any other site. If it contains any other number (or multiple
numbers) the site at that index is linked to sites at the index of the listed
numbers and this site is to be retained when removing linkage. If it contains
NA the site is linked to at least one other sited and this site should be
excluded to remove the linkage.

Armed with this knowledge let's take a look at the link_list we generated previously:

```{r advanced_llist}
print(llist, n = 10)
```

Here you can see that the 1st site in the **masked** vcf (which is actually site
1024 in the original vcf, according to the translation layer) is linked to the
8th site in the masked vcf. In order to remove this link, the `mask(vcf, llist)`
function will mask the 8th site and keep the 1st. Moving on, the 2nd site is
linked to some other site (if we look further down we can see it is linked to
the 9th site) and the `mask()` function will mask this site in order to remove
this link. Finally, the 3rd site in the masked vcf is not linked to any other
site and thus will not be masked when using the `mask()` function.
